1.pericope_label: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men: a man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease
debates: Why the owner cannot eat of his own: Clarke makes it a general truth that the power of enjoying is a separate gift from the thing enjoyed, while Wesley makes the withholding judicial, God having given the man up to a base and covetous mind.
Whether this is a new evil or the same one: Gill notes that one old version makes it a second and different evil and thinks that wrong, the covetousness of the preceding chapter being still in view.
outliers: Henry compares the wealth of a body politic to blood, which if it stagnates instead of circulating will be of ill consequence, and says the public is damaged by penuriousness as much as by prodigality.
Ellicott prefers heavy upon to common among in the first line.
Keil and Delitzsch refuse a rendering giving there is nothing wanting to him, and say the stranger who takes the estate is certainly not the legal heir.
themes: An estate passing to no heir

3.pericope_label: If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he. For he cometh in with vanity, and departeth in darkness ... Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?
debates: Why the man has no burial: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both suspect the Preacher has an actual occurrence in mind, since the detail does not follow from the rest, while Clarke makes the want of a grave deliberate, the man grudging himself a monument.

Who is described in the fourth verse: Gill sets out three possibilities, the untimely birth, the covetous man, or both compared in the same terms, without settling them; Ellicott decides for the untimely birth.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar who took the clause about burial for a marginal note that had wandered into the text, and answer that its very air of accident suggests real facts fitted into an imagined portrait.

Keil and Delitzsch concede that a long joyless life is worthless, then mark a limit in their author, saying he does not appear to know that a life deepened into fellowship with God is itself the highest good.
Gill reports a Jewish reading making the phrase a thousand thousand, which he thinks wrong, and an Arabic version giving many thousand years.
themes: A full house and an empty life
The unborn preferred to the living

7.pericope_label: All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. For what hath the wise more than the fool? what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this is also vanity and vexation of spirit
debates: Whether the mouth and the soul are set in contrast: Keil and Delitzsch refuse a reading that makes them organs of sensual and of spiritual joy, saying it brings out of the text what it wishes to find there, and hold that the stomach could have been named instead of the soul.

What the wandering of the desire means: Keil and Delitzsch reject a rendering giving an impulse of the appetite and take it as a roving to a distance, while Clarke stops at the literal travelling of the soul and asks, without answering, whether it refers to the state of separate spirits.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report that the old translators contribute nothing to the eighth verse, reject a Jewish reading that takes the living for the blessed future, and cannot make the man who walks before the living a public figure without absurdity.
Ellicott grants that the phrase means knowing how to conduct oneself, but says it is not obvious why this should be limited to the poor.
Henry reports an alternative rendering of the seventh verse, that though a man’s labour fall out exactly to his own mind his desire is still not satisfied.

10.pericope_label: That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it is man: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he. Seeing there be many things that increase vanity, what is man the better? For who knoweth what is good for man in this life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun?
debates: Who is named in the tenth verse: Gill and Clarke both find the first man there, while Gill reports that some refer the words to the second man, the Lord from heaven, and that one old version reads not that which has been but that which shall be.

Whether the eleventh verse speaks of things or of words: Keil and Delitzsch argue for words, since the contending of the previous verse is carried on in speech, and name commentators who take the other view; Ellicott allows the rendering without pressing it.
outliers: Ellicott calls the tenth verse difficult and says plainly that he prefers one translation among several, adding that the word for the stronger party occurs only in the Chaldee portions of the Bible and in later Hebrew.
Keil and Delitzsch reject a repunctuation made against the accents that would give, it is known that if one is a man he cannot contend, and call the construction it requires impossible.
Keil and Delitzsch find in the eleventh verse a trace of the schools existing in the author’s own time, recalling the controversy between the parties over human freedom and divine absoluteness.
Clarke says futurity is with God, that a man living wishes to know what is before him and a man dying what will be after him, and that God in mercy will reveal neither.
themes: Neither present good nor future known
